learn.hook: Your street light is broken, the village pond is silting up, and the primary school needs a new toilet. Would you rather wait for Delhi, or walk to your panchayat office?
points: Local government is government at the village and district level (panchayats) and the town and city level (municipalities). It is the level of government closest to ordinary people.
It deals with everyday matters: drinking water, sanitation, local roads, primary schools, street lights, markets.
Benefits: people can participate directly; local knowledge leads to better decisions; problems are solved faster and more cheaply; it deepens democracy through democratic decentralisation.
Decentralisation means transferring powers and resources from higher levels of government to local bodies.
Activity idea: when a dispute over the use of a common village land is settled by the villagers themselves in a gram sabha, it shows how local democracy can resolve conflicts with local knowledge.

example.q: Villagers disagree on whether to use a common plot as a playground or a cattle shed. Why might a local body settle this better than the State government?
steps: Local leaders know the village's needs and the history of the plot.
Villagers can attend the meeting and voice their views directly.
The decision can be taken quickly and its fairness seen by all.
example.answer: Local knowledge, direct participation and speed make local bodies better placed.

learn.reallife: When your ward councillor arranges for a new water pipeline in your colony, you experience local government at work.

topics.title: Growth of local government in India

learn.hook: Village assemblies called sabhas existed in ancient India. But it took until 1992 for panchayats to be written firmly into the Constitution. What happened in between?
points: Early history: ancient sabhas and village panchayats; in the colonial period, Lord Ripon's resolution of 1882 promoted local self-government, and the Government of India Act 1919 led to village panchayats in several provinces.

Gandhi's idea of gram swaraj saw strong, self-reliant villages as the foundation of democracy. In the Constitution, local government became a State subject, and Article 40 (a Directive Principle) asks the State to organise village panchayats.
After independence: the Community Development Programme (1952); the Balwantrai Mehta Committee (1957) recommended a three-tier panchayati raj system.
Weaknesses: local bodies lacked funds, elections were irregular or postponed, and they depended heavily on State governments.
The Ashok Mehta Committee (1977) and the L.M. Singhvi Committee (1986) pushed for strengthening panchayats, and the L.M. Singhvi Committee suggested constitutional recognition.

example.q: Put these in order: Balwantrai Mehta Committee, Lord Ripon's resolution, Community Development Programme, L.M. Singhvi Committee.
example.answer: Ripon 1882 → CDP 1952 → Balwantrai Mehta 1957 → L.M. Singhvi 1986.

learn.reallife: Many villages still remember Gandhiji's dream of gram swaraj on 2 October, when gram sabhas across India meet on Gandhi Jayanti.

learn.hook: Since 1993, every Indian village is part of a constitutionally protected three-storey building of democracy: Gram Panchayat, Panchayat Samiti, Zila Parishad.
points: The 73rd Amendment (1992) dealt with rural local bodies (panchayats); the 74th Amendment dealt with urban local bodies. Both came into force in 1993.

Three-tier structure: Gram Panchayat (village level), Panchayat Samiti or Mandal (block or intermediate level) and Zila Parishad (district level). Smaller States (population under 20 lakh) need not have the intermediate tier.
Gram Sabha: all adult voters registered in the village; it is the base of the panchayati raj system.
Elections: members of all three tiers are directly elected; each body has a five-year term. If a body is dissolved early, fresh elections must be held within six months.
Elections are conducted by an independent State Election Commission in each State, not by the Election Commission of India.

example.q: A Zila Parishad is dissolved by the State government on 1 January 2025. By when must fresh elections be held?
steps: The 73rd Amendment requires fresh elections within six months of dissolution.
The State Election Commission conducts the election.
example.answer: Within six months, i.e. by 1 July 2025.

learn.reallife: A State Election Commission notice for panchayat polls, with separate ballots for ward member, Panchayat Samiti and Zila Parishad, shows all three tiers being elected directly.

topics.title: 73rd Amendment: reservations, subjects, finances and PESA

learn.hook: Lakhs of women have become sarpanches and panchayat members since 1993 — thanks to a single clause that reserved one-third of seats and chairperson posts for them.
points: Reservations: one-third of seats and of chairperson (adhyaksha) posts at all levels are reserved for women. Seats are reserved for SC and ST in proportion to their population; States may also reserve seats for OBCs. Many States have raised women's reservation to 50%.

Transfer of subjects: the Eleventh Schedule lists 29 subjects (e.g. agriculture, minor irrigation, drinking water, rural housing, primary and secondary education, health and sanitation, poverty alleviation) that States may transfer to panchayats.
Because these subjects are on the State List, the actual transfer depends on State laws.
State Finance Commission: appointed every five years to review the financial position of local bodies and recommend the sharing of revenue between the State and local bodies.
PESA Act 1996 (Panchayats (Extension to Scheduled Areas) Act): extends panchayat provisions to Scheduled Areas while respecting tribal customs and traditions and community resources.

example.q: A Gram Panchayat has 15 seats. What is the minimum number reserved for women?
steps: The 73rd Amendment reserves not less than one-third of seats for women.
So at least 5 seats are reserved for women (more in States with 50% reservation).

learn.reallife: In States with 50% reservation for women in panchayats, every second sarpanch seat can be held by a woman — changing village leadership across India.

learn.hook: Nearly a third of Indians live in towns and cities. Who fixes their potholes, water pipes and garbage collection? Since 1993, constitutionally protected urban local bodies.
points: The 74th Amendment (1992) gave constitutional status to urban local bodies (municipalities), and came into force in 1993.
Three types: Municipal Corporations for larger urban areas, Municipal Councils (municipalities) for smaller urban areas, and Nagar Panchayats for areas in transition from rural to urban.
Many features match the 73rd Amendment: direct elections, five-year terms, reservation for women (one-third), SC and ST, State Election Commission and State Finance Commission.

The Twelfth Schedule lists 18 subjects for urban local bodies, e.g. urban planning, regulation of land use, roads and bridges, water supply, public health and sanitation, fire services, slum improvement, burial and cremation grounds.
Larger municipalities also have ward committees so citizens can participate at the neighbourhood level.

example.q: Classify: (a) Mumbai; (b) a small town of 60,000; (c) a fast-growing village becoming a town.
steps: (b) A smaller urban area → Municipal Council (municipality).
(c) An area in transition from rural to urban → Nagar Panchayat.
example.answer: (a) Municipal Corporation, (b) Municipal Council, (c) Nagar Panchayat.

topics.title: How well have the amendments worked?

learn.hook: Today India has lakhs of elected local representatives, and a large share of them are women. But many still wait for real money and power.
points: Since 1993, regular local elections have been held in most States, producing a huge number of elected representatives, including many women, SC and ST members.
Women's participation has grown: lakhs of women serve as members and chairpersons, and many have become confident leaders in village and town affairs.
Problems: limited funds of their own; heavy dependence on grants from State and Union governments; State governments have transferred few subjects and staff, so real devolution is limited.
Local bodies often implement schemes designed elsewhere rather than plan their own priorities.
Evaluation: the amendments created a strong democratic base, but more fiscal and administrative autonomy is needed for genuine self-government.

example.q: A sarpanch says: 'We are elected, but we have no money and no staff.' Which weaknesses of implementation does this show?
steps: 'No money' → limited own funds and dependence on grants.
'No staff' → States have not transferred staff and functions.
Together these show limited real devolution despite regular elections.
example.answer: Limited funds and incomplete devolution of functions and staff.

learn.reallife: When a woman sarpanch in Rajasthan or Bihar gets a new road or school toilet built, it shows the transformative side of the 73rd Amendment.
